summary: Busulfan is a bifunctional alkylating agent used (IV, with cyclophosphamide) as a conditioning regimen before allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for chronic myelogenous leukemia. It alkylates DNA, producing profound and prolonged myelosuppression - a BOXED WARNING - so transplant rescue is mandatory. Anticonvulsant and antiemetic premedication is required, and patients must be monitored for seizures and hepatic veno-occlusive disease.
indications: In combination with cyclophosphamide, as a conditioning regimen prior to allogeneic hematopoietic progenitor (stem) cell transplantation for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML)

dosage.d: 0.8 mg/kg (ideal or actual body weight, whichever is lower) IV every 6 hours
dosage.n: Days -7 to -4; 2-hour infusion via central line

dosage.d: Cyclophosphamide 60 mg/kg IV over 1 hour on each of 2 days
dosage.n: Begin no sooner than 6 h after the 16th busulfan dose

dosage.d: Anticonvulsant (benzodiazepine, phenytoin, valproic acid, or levetiracetam) plus antiemetic

admin: Administer ONLY as a diluted intravenous infusion via a central venous catheter - never IV push or bolus
Pre-medicate with an anticonvulsant and an antiemetic before and during therapy
Hematopoietic progenitor cell transplant is mandatory to rescue from myelosuppression
Handle as a hazardous cytotoxic agent using appropriate precautions
moa: Busulfan is a bifunctional alkylating agent with two labile methanesulfonate groups attached to a four-carbon alkyl chain. In aqueous media it hydrolyzes, releasing methanesulfonate groups and forming reactive carbonium ions that alkylate DNA (notably forming interstrand and intrastrand cross-links). The resulting DNA damage disrupts replication and transcription, accounting for its cytotoxic, myeloablative effect.

absolute: History of hypersensitivity to busulfan or any component
Absence of a definitive diagnosis where myeloablation is not indicated (do not use without confirmed indication)
relative: Prior cranial irradiation or seizure history (seizure risk)
Hepatic impairment / risk of veno-occlusive disease
monitor: Complete blood counts daily during treatment
Hepatic function and signs of veno-occlusive disease

preg: Busulfan can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during and after treatment; males should also use contraception. It can impair fertility (ovarian failure, azoospermia).
lact: It is not known whether busulfan is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, breastfeeding should be discontinued during therapy.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established; busulfan is primarily hepatically metabolized. Use caution and monitor in renal impairment as data are limited.
hepatic: Use with caution; busulfan is extensively metabolized by the liver and is associated with hepatotoxicity and hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), particularly at high transplant doses. Monitor liver function closely.

major: Acetaminophen (reduced glutathione may decrease busulfan clearance - avoid within 72 h before/with busulfan)
Phenytoin (increases busulfan clearance/lowers exposure - affects dosing if used as anticonvulsant)
moderate: Other myelosuppressive or hepatotoxic agents (additive toxicity)
interactions.food: IV formulation; not affected by food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additional hepatic and CNS burden
interactions.diagnostics: Causes marked declines in all blood cell lines; may elevate liver enzymes/bilirubin

serious: Prolonged pancytopenia with risk of infection and bleeding
Hepatic veno-occlusive disease / sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
Cardiac tamponade (reported with high-dose use, esp. in thalassemia)

monitoring: Daily complete blood count with differential and platelets during treatment
Hepatic function tests; vigilance for veno-occlusive disease
Neurologic monitoring for seizures (with anticonvulsant prophylaxis)
Pulmonary symptoms (cough, dyspnea) for busulfan lung toxicity
counsel: This is a powerful chemotherapy used to prepare you for a stem cell transplant
It causes a severe, expected drop in blood counts - infection and bleeding precautions are essential
You will receive medicines to prevent seizures and nausea
Use effective contraception; it can harm a fetus and may impair future fertility
Report fever, unusual bleeding/bruising, breathing problems, or yellowing of the skin immediately
pk: Myelosuppression develops within days of conditioning dosing
IV: plasma peak at end of the 2-hour infusion
Myelosuppression is prolonged; recovery depends on transplant engraftment
Store ampules/vials refrigerated at 2-8 C; do not freeze (per product labeling)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: causes severe and prolonged myelosuppression - hematopoietic progenitor cell transplant is REQUIRED to prevent fatal complications
Seizure prophylaxis with an anticonvulsant is mandatory; busulfan lowers the seizure threshold
Therapeutic drug monitoring of busulfan AUC is often used to individualize dosing and reduce VOD risk
Avoid acetaminophen near busulfan dosing - glutathione depletion can reduce clearance and increase toxicity
missed: Busulfan is given as a strictly timed inpatient transplant conditioning schedule by oncology staff; missed or delayed doses are managed by the transplant team and are not self-administered.
overdose: There is no antidote; busulfan is dialyzable, and dialysis has been used. Overdose intensifies myelosuppression and risks severe pancytopenia, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and seizures. Management is supportive: hematologic support (transfusions, growth factors), infection prophylaxis/treatment, anticonvulsants, and consideration of dialysis to enhance removal.
